question: to the Commission Lídia Pereira (PPE), Sebastião Bugalho (PPE), Paulo Cunha (PPE), Paulo do Nascimento Cabral (PPE) Subject:

On 9 April 2026, the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) and the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) published a joint document1 proposing a European risk-sharing mechanism for natural disasters, based on two pillars: a European insurance pool financed by risk-based premiums and a loan-based backstop for extreme events, with an estimated capacity of between EUR 10 billion and 65 billion. The document estimates that between 50 % and 75 % of economic losses from natural disasters remain uninsured, and it identifies Portugal among the Member States with the biggest protection gaps, particularly in terms of wildfires, floods, heatwaves and earthquake risk. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission intend to follow up on the EIOPA/ESM proposal with legislative action and, if so, what would the timeline be, and how would it link to existing national regimes or those under preparation, including the future Fundo de Catástrofes português (‘Portuguese Disaster Fund’)?
How does the Commission intend to complement this supply-driven mechanism with demand-side measures, including risk literacy and investment in prevention and adaptation?
What role does it see for the capital market in strengthening the capacity of the European pool?

https://www.eiopa.europa.eu/document/download/c8be856b-b358-4b68-9c3480672f2e4c28_en?filename=ESM-EIOPA%20Discussion%20Paper%20-%20Sharing%20the%20risk%20%20A%20European%20approach%20to%20natural%20catastrophe%20risk%20management.pdf. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The Commission’s priority is to engage with insurance distributors and insurance undertakings on the role that they can play in raising household awareness of potential options to increase insurance coverage for climate-related losses. The Commission is of the view that enhanced awareness regarding the increased frequency, and sometimes severity, of climate related losses and, to that end, enhanced financial literacy, will play an essential role in efforts to narrow the climate protection gap in the EU. The Commission is also investigating, together with the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, whether premium benefits for precautionary action taken by households could play a role in raising awareness of climate risk and reduce its potential impacts. The discussion paper published by the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority and the European Stability Mechanism provides technical input to inform policy discussions on natural catastrophe risk management. Such input, as well as initiatives emerging at national level, as for example Portugal’s recent announcement to establish a national disaster fund, will feed the Commission’s reflections in this area. The Commission aims to strengthen preparedness across society by improving public awareness of risks and how to reduce them. As part of the Preparedness Union Strategy1, particular focus is placed on population preparedness and on improving access to reliable risk information, for example through tools like the Risk Data Hub. In addition, the Commission supports prevention and adaptation through its broader policy and funding framework, including through the adoption of the Preparedness by Design principle.
